content: Vaccination involves the administration of specific antigenic components that are relatively harmless but capable of inducing protective immunity against corresponding infectious agents in vaccinated individuals. In clinical practice, the terms vaccination and immunization are often used interchangeably. Vaccination is highly effective in preventing certain infections and is associated with minimal adverse reactions. It can prevent illnesses, disabilities, and deaths caused by vaccine-preventable diseases such as cervical cancer, diphtheria, hepatitis B, measles, mumps, pertussis, pneumonia, polio, rotavirus diarrhea, rubella, and tetanus. Vaccines work by mimicking an infection, which stimulates the immune system to produce T-lymphocytes and antibodies without causing illness. Immunization currently prevents an estimated 2 to 3 million deaths annually, but an additional 5 million deaths could be avoided if global vaccination coverage were improved. Despite this, 4 million infants worldwide still lack access to basic vaccines. Vaccines can be composed of live but weakened forms of pathogens (bacteria or viruses), killed or inactivated forms of these pathogens, or purified materials such as proteins. Benjamin Jesty is recognized as one of the first individuals to use cowpox to artificially induce immunity to smallpox during the 1774 epidemic. The term vaccination was first introduced by Edward Jenner in 1796, and Louis Pasteur later expanded on this principle in his groundbreaking work in microbiology. The term vaccination derives from the Latin word vacca, meaning cow, as the first vaccine was derived from the cowpox virus, which provided immunity to smallpox, a highly contagious and deadly disease. The World Health Organization (WHO) led the global effort to eradicate smallpox, with the last naturally occurring case reported in Somalia in 1977. Vaccine-Preventable Diseases and Classifications Passive Immunization Passive immunization involves the transfer of pre-made antibodies to individuals at risk of acquiring a specific disease. This immunity can occur naturally during pregnancy through the transplacental transfer of maternal antibodies to the fetus. Artificial passive immunization is typically administered via pre-made immunoglobulins to individuals at risk of certain diseases. Human Immune Globulin (IG) Human immune globulin is derived from healthy individuals and is a concentrated solution of antibodies, primarily IgG. It is administered intramuscularly (IM), requiring up to 48 hours to reach maximum serum concentration, with a half-life of approximately three weeks. Early administration enhances its effectiveness, but IG provides only temporary protection. Diseases for which human immune globulins are available include hepatitis A, measles, immunoglobulin deficiency, varicella (in immunocompromised patients when varicella-zoster IG is unavailable), and rubella exposure during the first trimester of pregnancy. Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) contains higher concentrations of antibodies and is administered intravenously. IVIG can prevent or mitigate diseases such as Kawasaki disease, pediatric HIV infection, chronic B-cell lymphocytic leukemia, primary immunodeficiencies, immune thrombocytopenia, and graft-versus-host disease. Subcutaneous immune globulin (SCIG) is designed for home use, particularly for patients with primary immunodeficiency. Hyperimmune Globulin Hyperimmune globulin is derived from human plasma containing high concentrations of specific antibodies. It is obtained from individuals recovering from natural infections or donors who have been artificially immunized. Hyperimmune globulins are available for diseases such as cytomegalovirus, varicella-zoster, hepatitis B, infant botulism, rabies, and tetanus. Monoclonal Antibodies Specific monoclonal antibodies can be used to combat infections. Currently, palivizumab is the only monoclonal antibody available, and it is effective against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Active Immunization Live Attenuated Vaccines Live attenuated vaccines are created by modifying a disease-causing virus or bacterium in a laboratory. The resulting vaccine organism retains the ability to replicate and induce immunity but typically does not cause illness. These vaccines are produced by growing the virus in tissue cultures that select for less virulent strains or through mutagenesis or targeted deletions in virulence-related genes. Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in immunocompromised individuals. Examples include the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine and the varicella (chickenpox) vaccine. Inactivated Vaccines Inactivated vaccines are produced by killing or inactivating the pathogen, most commonly viruses. An example of this type of vaccine is the inactivated polio vaccine. Toxoid Vaccines Toxoid vaccines are effective against bacteria that produce toxins. These vaccines contain weakened toxins produced by specific bacteria. The DTaP vaccine, for example, includes diphtheria and tetanus toxoids. Subunit Vaccines Subunit vaccines contain only essential parts of bacteria or viruses, not the entire germ. Because they include only the necessary antigens and exclude other molecules, side effects are less common. The pertussis component of the DTaP vaccine is an example of a subunit vaccine. Conjugate Vaccines Conjugate vaccines are effective against bacteria with polysaccharides in their cell wall components. Polysaccharides may elicit a weaker immune response, but conjugate vaccines link these polysaccharides to antigens that the immune system responds to robustly. This linkage helps immature immune systems recognize the coating and develop an immune response. An example of this type of vaccine is the Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) vaccine. Adverse Reactions to Vaccines Adverse reactions to vaccines can be categorized into two major groups: allergic reactions and severe reportable reactions. Allergic Reactions Immediate Reactions: These are IgE-mediated reactions that occur within minutes of vaccine administration. Delayed Reactions: These appear several hours or even days after administration and are typically non-IgE-mediated. Immediate Reactions Anaphylaxis, though rare, is a critical immediate reaction. Healthcare providers must recognize its symptoms and be prepared for prompt treatment. Other common but less severe immediate reactions include: Cutaneous Symptoms: Flushing, itching, urticaria, and angioedema. Respiratory Symptoms: Nasal discharge, nasal congestion, changes in voice quality, throat closure or choking sensation, stridor, cough, wheezing, and dyspnea. Cardiovascular Symptoms: Faintness, syncope, altered mental status, palpitations, and hypotension. Delayed Reactions Common delayed reactions to vaccines include: Fever: Fever is a common post-vaccination reaction and should not deter future vaccinations. Local Reactions: Swelling and erythema at the injection site are common and can be managed with a cold compress. Serum Sickness and Serum Sickness-Like Reactions Vasovagal Reactions Vasovagal reactions, such as fainting, hypotension, pallor, diaphoresis, weakness, nausea, vomiting, bradycardia, and, in severe cases, loss of consciousness, may occur after vaccination. Reactions to Vaccine Components Vaccine components such as gelatin, egg proteins, cow's milk, thimerosal, aluminum, and phenoxyethanol, which are used as preservatives, may cause adverse reactions ranging from fever or skin reactions to severe reactions requiring skin testing before future administration. Severe Reportable Reactions Anaphylaxis or anaphylactic shock occurring within seven days of any vaccine administration should be reported.
